episodes.178466: A longwave trough exited the Intermountain West into the Central and Southern Plains on April 15th, which reinforced a cold front southeast into Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Southwest Arkansas during the afternoon. Hot and humid air spread north across the region from the Gulf of Mexico ahead of the front with the northward advance of a warm front, with temperatures climbing into the upper 80s and lower 90s areawide. These abnormally hot and humid conditions resulted in moderate to very unstable conditions ahead of the front, as large scale ascent increased ahead of the ejecting trough along and just ahead of the approaching cold front. As a result, scattered to numerous strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening hours across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana, and produced multiple instances of large hail across portions of Southwest Arkansas before exiting the area during the mid-evening hours.

episodes.178615: Two distinct severe storms crossed southern Illinois during the afternoon and evening. During the afternoon, an isolated severe storm tracked east across the Ohio River counties from near Cairo to near Metropolis and then the Golconda area. This storm produced swaths of quarter-size hail and a few damaging wind gusts. During the evening, a line of severe storms moved east across the Interstate 57 corridor from around Marion to the Mount Vernon area. Isolated large hail and damaging winds accompanied these storms. The storms formed along and ahead of a cold front that trailed southward from a low pressure system over the western Great Lakes. The air mass remained moderately unstable into the evening hours, when mixed-layer capes decreased to around 1000 j/kg. Effective bulk wind shear averaged around 35 knots in the evening.
episodes.178618: A loosely organized cluster of thunderstorms evolved into a broken line of thunderstorms as they moved east from the Ozark foothills into the Poplar Bluff area. Wind damage occurred with a couple of the storms, especially over Ripley County. Dime to nickel-size hail was also reported with a few storms. The storms formed along a cold front that trailed southward from a low pressure system over the western Great Lakes. The air mass remained moderately unstable into the evening hours, when mixed-layer capes decreased to around 1500 j/kg. Effective bulk wind shear averaged from 35 to 40 knots in the evening.
episodes.178787: Weak upper level disturbances migrated across south Florida, which including daytime heating, brought strong thunderstorms to Lake Okeechobee on April 16th.
episodes.178799: The spring snow melt of 2023 saw many areas of flooding over North Dakota due to a record deep snow pack and relatively fast melt. Multiple counties experienced infrastructure damage due to the flooding. In addition, during the morning hours of April 16, a flood death (direct) occurred as a 54 year old female was driving a 2004 Ford Escape along ND Highway 66 near the intersection of 47th Avenue NE, to the northwest of Mylo, Rolette County. The road was covered with water and ice due to snow melt flooding, and temperatures below freezing. The driver lost control of the vehicle, which went into the north ditch, rolled and overturned onto its roof in the flooded ditch. The driver died (direct).
episodes.178849: A deeper than average snow pack from northern Minnesota into northern Wisconsin underwent a rapid melt through much of April from unseasonably warm temperatures combined with multiple rain events. This resulted in increased water levels and significant flooding for the entire length of the local Mississippi River, with most sites climbing to their third to fifth highest crests on record. A significant mid-April rain and snow event resulted in the Governor of Wisconsin issuing a State of Emergency declaration for flooding on April 16, 2023. Initial flood warnings were issued in mid April with peak stages realized in late April. The highest above flood stage was Lynxville Dam at 5.26 ft over flood stage.
episodes.178852: A deeper than average snow pack from northern Minnesota into northern Wisconsin underwent a rapid melt through much of April from unseasonably warm temperatures combined with multiple rain events. This resulted in increased water levels and significant flooding for the entire length of the local Mississippi River, with most sites climbing to their third to fifth highest crests on record. Initial flood warnings were issued in mid April with peak stages realized in late April. The highest above flood stage was Winona Dam at 5.81 ft over flood stage.
episodes.178867: Snowmelt resulted in flooding along the James River and its associated tributaries. The National Weather Service recorded an April record snow depth of 26 inches in Aberdeen on the 5th. This was followed by near normal temperatures through the latter half of the month of April. This relatively mild warmup resulted in snowmelt on top of frozen ground, and forced most of the melt into the waterways. River gauges near Columbia peaked just below major flood stage at 17.85 feet on April 30th and near Stratford just below moderate flood stage with 16.75 feet on April 30th. The gauge near Ashton peaked well above major flood stage at 19.91 feet on April 21st, which overtopped one of the bridges and impacted another near the gauge site. The gauge near Redfield peaked at 22.3 feet on April 22nd, just above moderate flood stage. Aside from the bridges and a few roads that were impacted, the main result of this high water was flooding of agricultural lands.

episodes.179163: Several strong to severe thunderstorms moved into eastern Missouri in the afternoon hours of April 15th. These storms were initially producing copious large hail, but rapidly transitioned into tornadic storms. The first tornado was associated with a supercell ahead of a congealing line of convection moving rapidly toward the Mississippi River. A portion of this line of storms rapidly surged eastward, resulting in numerous tornadoes in Jefferson county in Missouri, and Monroe, Madison, St. Clair, and Washington counties in Illinois. In total, 12 tornadoes have been identified, including 3 EF-1s, 6 EF-0s, and 3 tornadoes of unknown intensity that produced no damage.

episodes.179316: The Mustinka River and its tributaries experienced flooding due to the rapid snowmelt in western Minnesota caused by frozen soils and a quick thaw in the second week of April. As a result, a large amount of snowmelt flowed into the waterways, leading to numerous county and township roads being submerged. To safeguard properties, many communities initiated sandbagging operations.

episodes.179593: As of 100 pm CDT, there were no storms yet. A sounding (temperature and dewpoint profile with height) revealed plenty of instability, and it was just a matter of time before the fireworks began. There was also a lot of dry air aloft, and forecasters knew this would likely lead to very large hail. Low level moisture driven into this dry environment overhead would create a lot of evaporation/cooling, making it easy for ice to form.||Between 230 pm and 330 pm CDT, thunderstorms developed rapidly in northwest and west central Arkansas. South and east, hen egg to tennis ball size hail occurred near Botkinburg (Van Buren County) and south of Joan (Clark County), and golf ball size stones occurred in Shirley (Van Buren County) and northwest of Tag (Pope County).||A 66 mph wind gust was measured at Newport (Jackson County), with a 61 mph gust at McCreanor (Lonoke County), and a gust to 60 mph at Russellville (Pope County). episodes.181380: A surface low drifted north-northeastward across east-central and northeastern WI during the morning through early evening of the 16th. Simultaneously, the low's trailing cold front swept eastward from east-central and southeastern WI, northeastern IL, and western IN to central Lake Erie and eastern OH. Within the warm sector ahead of the cold front, multicell showers and thunderstorms persisted generally north-northeastward across western Lake Erie and produced a few gale-force and storm-force peak convective gusts along and near the lakeshore in northwest OH. This convection occurred in an environment with weak MUCAPE, weak DCAPE, and moderate effective bulk shear. The strong to severe gusts were likely the result of precipitation transporting much stronger winds aloft to the surface.
episodes.181391: A surface low drifted north-northeastward across east-central and northeastern WI during the morning through early evening of the 16th. Simultaneously, the low's trailing cold front swept eastward from east-central and southeastern WI, northeastern IL, and western IN to central Lake Erie and eastern OH. Within the warm sector ahead of the cold front, a cluster of multicell showers and thunderstorms persisted north-northeastward and generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage in the Elyria area during the late afternoon of the 16th. This convection occurred in an environment with weak MUCAPE, weak DCAPE, and moderate effective bulk shear. The damaging gusts were likely the result of precipitation transporting much stronger winds aloft to the surface.

Significant upstream runoff from the combination of rainfall and rapidly melting snow pushed the Mississippi River at Winona into flood stage on April 16th. A crest of 18.81 ft occurred on April 26th, 5.81 ft over flood stage.
Significant upstream runoff from the combination of rainfall and melting snow led to the Mississippi River at Fountain City rising over Highway 35, closing Main St from April 25th to 26th.

Significant upstream runoff from the combination of rainfall and melting snow pushed the Mississippi River at Trempealeau into flood stage on April 16th. The crest of 651.01 ft above sea level on April 25 was 4.01 ft over flood stage. Lake Road abutting the Mississippi River was closed due to water over the roadway.

Significant upstream runoff from the combination of rainfall and rapidly melting snow pushed the Mississippi River at Lake City into flood stage on April 16th. A crest of 18.98 ft occurred on April 24th, 2.98 ft over flood stage.
A house had minor siding damage.
Several trees were blown down south of Athens. Power lines that fell in accompaniment led to power outages in the area.

A National Weather Service Melbourne damage survey confirms that|a brief EF-0 tornado touched down initially in the River Groves|mobile home community in Micco. The tornado continued to the east-|southeast into the Summit Cove Condominiums complex before|crossing US-1 and emerging into the Indian River Lagoon near the|Sebastian River Marina and Boatyard. The tornado was on the|ground for approximately 0.5 miles, had a maximum width of|approximately 100 yards, and peak winds estimated between 65-75|mph.||Damage was first noted near Love Ct. where the tornado touched|down at approximately 536 pm EDT. Brevard County Emergency|Management conducted an initial assessment and documented between|25-30 structures with at least minor damage in the River Groves|community, primarily along Love Ct., Cherish Dr., and River Groves|Dr. These homes suffered partial damage to carports, awnings,|siding, and skirting. Additionally, several structures lost|portions of their roof when the attached carport or porch awnings|were torn away from the home.||The tornado continued east-southeast toward the Summit Cove|Condominiums complex where some damage was noted to trees near|the clubhouse, as well as siding on nearby homes, on Summit Cove|Dr. The system crossed US-1 before emerging into the Indian River|Lagoon near the Sebastian River Marina & Boatyard, where several|boats were moved from their storage rack. An eyewitness indicates the|tornado briefly became a waterspout before dissipating.||There are no known direct injuries or fatalities as a result of|the tornado.
